Uttara University · Undergraduate Thesis

Perovskite/TOPCon Tandem Solar Cells — a SCAPS-1D simulation study targeting above 33.05%

A wide-bandgap perovskite top cell stacked on a silicon TOPCon bottom cell can pass the single-junction limit — if the two subcells are modelled honestly. We reproduced the published devices in SCAPS-1D, combined them in series, and reached 33.64% tandem efficiency, above Shrivastava et al.'s reported 33.05%.

Research Overview

Why a perovskite–silicon tandem?

A single solar cell wastes the energy of photons far above its bandgap. A tandem splits the job: a wide-bandgap perovskite top cell (bandgap 1.65–1.68 eV in this work) absorbs the blue and green part of sunlight, and the silicon TOPCon bottom cell absorbs the red and infrared light that passes through. The two cells are connected in series, so their voltages add while the current is set by the weaker subcell.

This page is organised in three parts. Part 1 presents Shrivastava et al.'s work and our reproduction of their perovskite/TOPCon tandem in SCAPS-1D, testing whether the published 33.05% can be matched or passed. Part 2 is the comparison: paper values set against our simulation values for Shrivastava, for the experimental base paper of Liao et al. (2025), and for the wide-bandgap devices surveyed in Cheng et al.'s review — so the tandem result is judged against real, current literature, not in isolation. Part 3 explains why we chose Shrivastava for this thesis.

Base paper — Liao et al. (2025)

Experimental perovskite/TOPCon tandem in Science Bulletin 70, 2997–3004. Top cell Cs0.22FA0.78Pb(I0.9Br0.1)3, bandgap 1.65 eV, single-junction efficiency 23.19%; tandem champion 30.90% (certified 30.83%). Our SCAPS-1D reproduction of its top cell is locked and documented.

Shrivastava et al. — the reproduced study

A SCAPS-1D tandem study reporting 33.05% — top cell 20.58%, filtered silicon bottom cell, series-combined tandem. One of only two papers we found with full supplementary data matching the Liao device family, which makes it a fair reproduction target.

Cheng et al. (2026) — wide-bandgap review

APL Energy 4, 011501: “Developing wide-bandgap perovskites for tandem solar cells.” Defines wide-bandgap as 1.65–2.0 eV, reports field-best tandem efficiency up to 35.0% and a best wide-bandgap single junction of 23.25% at 1.67 eV — the benchmark for our comparison run.

Part 1

Shrivastava's work — the tandem reproduction

Shrivastava et al. modelled a perovskite top cell on a silicon bottom cell entirely in SCAPS-1D and reported a 33.05% tandem. We rebuilt their two subcells with the same discipline used throughout this thesis: paper-given values are never changed just to force a match, one variable moves at a time, and every run is re-verified before its numbers are read. The full step-by-step method is set out in the Method section further down this page.

Shrivastava et al. · Reproduction

Shrivastava tandem reproduction

Rebuild the paper's two subcells in SCAPS-1D and combine them exactly the way the paper's own supplementary script does.

  • Top cell: 500 nm perovskite absorber, series resistance 5 Ω·cm² — 20.26% vs the paper's 20.58%
  • Bottom cell: silicon cell under the filtered spectrum (light after passing through 500 nm of perovskite) — short-circuit current density matches the paper within 0.05 mA/cm²
  • Combination: voltages added at the same current, Vtandem = Vtop + Vbottom; current set by the bottom cell
  • Honest note: our tandem voltage is higher than the paper's because the model has lower recombination — reported as a model property, not hidden
Final tandem: 2.079 V · 19.876 mA/cm² · 81.40% · 33.64% — above the paper's 33.05%

How it was done, in brief: the tandem needs 11 layers and two different spectra, so it is run as two SCAPS-1D files — the top cell under full AM1.5G, the bottom cell under the spectrum filtered through 500 nm of perovskite — and the two exported current–voltage curves are then combined in series, voltages added at the same current. This is the same approach as the paper's own supplementary script.

Part 1 · Method in Full

How the tandem is simulated in SCAPS-1D

SCAPS-1D holds at most 7 layers per file, and this tandem needs 11 (5 in the top cell, 6 in the bottom cell). The two subcells also see different light — the top cell gets the full AM1.5G spectrum, the bottom cell only what the perovskite lets through. So the tandem is run as two files and combined in series, the same approach as the paper's own supplementary script.

STEP 1

Top cell run

Perovskite top cell under the full AM1.5G spectrum, 1000 W/m², 300 K. Current–voltage sweep from 0 to 1.40 V in 71 points. The J–V curve is exported as an .iv file.

STEP 2

Filtered spectrum

The spectrum that reaches the silicon is built with the Beer–Lambert law through the perovskite absorber (500 nm), using real silicon absorption data (Green 2008).

STEP 3

Bottom cell run

Silicon bottom cell simulated under that filtered spectrum only, and its J–V curve exported the same way.

STEP 4

Series combination

A short Python script adds the two voltages at the same current to build the tandem curve. It does no new simulation — only the series addition.

Vtandem(J) = Vtop(J) + Vbottom(J)   ·   Jsctandem = min(Jsctop, Jscbottom)   ·   FF and η are read from the combined curve

Part 3

Why we chose Shrivastava

Several tandem papers were checked during the literature search. Shrivastava et al. was chosen as the reproduction and improvement target for four reasons.

01

Our simulation matched its values closely

The reproduction landed close to the paper on every device: top cell 20.26% vs 20.58% (a gap of only 0.32 percentage points), the filtered bottom cell's short-circuit current density 19.876 mA/cm² vs 19.83 — within 0.05 mA/cm² — and the tandem at 33.64% vs 33.05%. A target our model can reproduce this closely is a target we can honestly try to improve.

02

It gives a complete SCAPS parameter set

Shrivastava et al. publish their full supplementary parameter tables, so every layer of the device can be built in SCAPS-1D from the paper itself. The experimental base paper, Liao et al., publishes no SCAPS parameter table at all — its model has to be calibrated from measured values, which is slower and leaves more parameters assumed.

03

Its perovskite is the closest to Liao's

The top cell uses a 1.68 eV perovskite with a Me-4PACz hole-selective layer — the closest match we found to the Liao device family (bandgap 1.65 eV, Cs0.22FA0.78Pb(I0.9Br0.1)3, Me-4PACz). Work done on the Shrivastava stack therefore transfers directly to the base-paper stack our thesis is built on.

04

It sets a clear target — 33.05%

The paper's reported tandem efficiency, 33.05%, is a concrete, published benchmark. Our thesis target is to go above it — and because the reproduction in Part 1 is verified, any improvement measured from it starts from a trustworthy baseline.

The target, in one line

Shrivastava et al. reported 33.05%. Our series-combined reproduction already reaches 33.64% — open-circuit voltage 2.079 V, short-circuit current density 19.876 mA/cm², fill factor 81.40% — and the thesis work continues from there, aiming to hold above 33.05% while closing the remaining gaps honestly.

Viva Preparation

Questions we are ready to answer

Why is the tandem simulated in two files instead of one?

SCAPS-1D allows at most 7 layers in one file; this tandem has 11 layers in total (5 in the top cell, 6 in the bottom cell). The two subcells also receive different light — full AM1.5G for the top cell, a filtered spectrum for the bottom cell — and one file cannot hold two spectra. So each subcell is run separately and the two are combined in series, which is also how the paper's own supplementary script works.

How were the two subcell values combined into one tandem value?

By series connection. The same current flows through both cells, so at each current the voltages add: Vtandem = Vtop + Vbottom. Read from the exported curves, the script extracts 1.2744 V + 0.8049 V = 2.0793 V. The current does not add; the tandem short-circuit current density is the smaller of the two, 19.876 mA/cm² (bottom-cell limited). Fill factor and efficiency are then read from the combined curve, not added.

Why is our tandem open-circuit voltage higher than the paper's?

The excess (2.079 V vs 2.02 V) comes from the bottom cell under the filtered spectrum (0.8054 V vs 0.72 V): the model has lower recombination than the paper's device. Interface defect densities are already at the paper's own supplementary value (1×10¹ cm⁻²), so we do not raise them just to pull the voltage down — the difference is reported, not hidden.

What does the combining script actually do?

Nothing beyond arithmetic on the two exported SCAPS-1D curves: it interpolates both curves onto a common current grid, adds the voltages point by point, and extracts open-circuit voltage, short-circuit current density, fill factor and efficiency. It runs no new simulation.

Why does the Liao reproduction still show a fill factor gap?

Against the paper's 83.73%, our locked point gives 73.66%. We ruled out, one variable at a time: absorber thickness, mobility, doping, interface defects, series and shunt resistance, contact work function and dielectric constant. The remaining explanation consistent with the evidence is field collapse across the absorber at the maximum power point. Because the paper does not report the parameters that would close it, the gap is stated as a limitation of the reproduction.
